The Man Behind Digha Mux Limited

Our
Story

A boy from Nnobi who opened radios in primary school, built a radio station in JSS3, and never stopped — until he changed the face of biomedical technology in Nigeria.

1972
Born May 6, 1972 · Nnobi, Anambra
Engr. Ubah Chuma
Founder · Inventor · Engineer · INV-INN
Who He Is

Born Curious.
Built to Invent.

Born May 6, 1972 · Nnobi, Anambra State

Long before the word "entrepreneur" was common in Nigeria, Engr. Ubah Chuma was already living it — in a small room in Nnobi, surrounded by electronic parts, wires, and the kind of curiosity that refuses to stay quiet.

He didn't just read about how things worked. He took them apart, rebuilt them, and then built things the world had never seen before — at an age when most children were still learning multiplication tables.

This is his story. And it is far from finished.

01
The Curious Child
Primary School · Nnobi
Where It All Began
He Was Wiring
Circuits in Primary 4

While other children were playing, young Ubah Chuma was doing electrical wiring in Primary 4. By Primary 6, he had moved on to repairing transistor radios — not just fixing them, but opening them up completely, studying every component, figuring out exactly how each part worked and why.

When he entered JSS1, he abandoned his school textbooks entirely and began reading encyclopaedias, physics books, books about NASA, astronomy, and the history of great inventions. While his classmates went to the library for English textbooks, he was hunting for the largest encyclopaedias he could find — absorbed by how things were made and how the world's great inventors thought.

"All his mates would be looking for intensive English books — but he would be looking for large books about encyclopaedias and inventions. He wasn't interested in what they were interested in."
The Workshop
A Room Full of
Experiments

By JSS2, Engr. Chuma had converted a room in his home into a full workshop — filled with electronic components, leftover accessories, wires, and parts from machines he had taken apart. It was here that the real work began.

He built apparatus to generate hydrogen gas from water, used it to fill balloons, and experimented with the same principles used in hydrogen airships. He built fridges. He built musical instruments. He was doing experiments that most university students had never attempted — and he was still in junior secondary school.

At an age when most children were just discovering homework, Engr. Chuma was extracting hydrogen from water and building working musical instruments in a makeshift workshop in Nnobi.

The Workshop
JSS2 · Nnobi
03
Nnobi Radio
JSS3 · Age ~14
The Moment That Changed Everything
He Built a
Radio Station
in JSS3

In JSS3 — still a teenager — Engr. Chuma built a working FM radio transmitter from scratch and launched what became known as Nnobi Radio Station. He built the transmitting mast, the speaker, the microphone — everything — by hand.

He then did something bold: he wrote a letter directly to the Local Government Chairman of Idemili (North and South were united at the time), signing it with the school's name — without telling his principal. One day, he was called to the principal's office to find five government officials sitting there, having driven all the way from the local government just to meet him.

They followed him to his house. He showed them his transmitter, his equipment, his creations. Three months later, they invited him to demonstrate everything at Children's Day in Ogidi — where he broadcast the entire event live on FM. Everyone in the area was tuning in.

He was a teenager with no funding, no mentor, and no university degree — yet he built a functioning FM radio station that broadcast across Nnobi. From scratch.
"
He set up his equipment at the field — both musical and his transmitter. He was broadcasting everything happening at Ogidi on FM. Everyone was tuning and listening.
— Children's Day, Ogidi · Idemili Local Government · Anambra State
The Scholarship
From Nnobi to
Enugu — On Scholarship

After the Children's Day demonstration, Engr. Chuma was invited to represent Idemili Local Government at a state exhibition in Enugu — which was then the capital of Anambra State. He transmitted FM from Enugu so powerfully that people back in Nnobi could tune in from home.

The Anambra State Government took notice. They wrote directly to Nnobi Boys School requesting his immediate transfer to Government Technical College (GTC) Enugu — with a full scholarship. He packed his bags and moved. He didn't live on campus — he rented a cheap room far from school and trekked to class every day. When the government changed and the scholarship was cut, he kept going anyway.

At GTC Enugu, he studied Radio & Television Communications, Electronic Devices & Circuits, and Basic Electricity. He scored 97% — the highest score in the school's history to that date. He contested the result because he knew he should have scored 100%. His Head of Department called on him whenever he had difficulty with a circuit. Teachers stopped questioning him — they already knew he would get it right.

97% — the highest score ever recorded at GTC Enugu. His HOD called on him for help. His teachers stopped asking him questions. He was also helping final-year University of Nigeria Nsukka students with their projects — and charging them for it.

05
The Struggle
IMT · ESUT · UNN
Against All Odds
He Never
Stopped Trying

After GTC Enugu, Engr. Chuma enrolled at the Institute of Management Technology (IMT). After two years, the money ran out — he dropped out. He tried again at Enugu State University of Science & Technology (ESUT). After one year, the money ran out again — he dropped out again.

Four years later, he received a letter from the University of Nigeria Nsukka (UNN). This time he was determined. He worked and studied at the same time — employed at the Equipment Maintenance and Development Centre at UNN, where they researched hospital equipment. It was here that everything came together: his engineering instincts, his medical curiosity, and the skills to build things that save lives.

After six years at UNN, he moved to Awka to start a new chapter. The Vice Chancellor of UNN kept writing letters urging him to return. He declined every one of them.

Dropped out twice. Kept going. Worked and studied simultaneously. Declined the Vice Chancellor's personal invitation to return. He had bigger things to build.
Building the Empire
Digha SAT First.
Then Biomedical.

Before Digha Biomedical, there was Digha SAT — a satellite television channel that Engr. Chuma launched and ran for four years. He eventually shut it down due to the rising dollar rate making operations unsustainable, but the ambition never died. Digha SAT is still being rebuilt for relaunch.

He also spent time at the Enugu Research Centre, where he designed a magnetizing machine — another invention that spoke to his relentless drive to engineer solutions where none existed before.

Finally, drawing on everything — his childhood radio stations, his GTC training, his years at UNN's Equipment Maintenance Centre — he opened Digha Biomedical. He began producing X-ray machines, electrosurgical machines, solar systems, electronic circuit boards, and more. All manufactured in Nigeria, ISO certified, and built to the same obsessive standard he has held since Primary 4.

Digha SAT came first. Then Digha Biomedical. Then a company that has now served 20+ hospitals across Nigeria — from Anambra to Abuja — for over 8 years and counting.
06
Digha Is Born
Awka · Anambra State · Nigeria
Giving Back

Donating Ultrasound to
General Hospital Nnobi

Engr. Ubah Chuma has never forgotten where he came from. In a powerful act of community, he donated an ultrasound machine to General Hospital Nnobi — in Idemili South Local Government Area, the very community where a young boy once built a radio station in a makeshift workshop.

It is the fullest expression of everything Digha stands for: not just building equipment for profit, but ensuring that Nigerian communities — especially the ones that shaped him — have access to the medical technology they deserve.
